text.p: These are the leading stories in the Zimbabwe press on Thursday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- State broadcaster Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation is technically broke and blames its predicament on cuts in government subsidies, its lifeline over the years, says a government-sanctioned report obtained by the Financial Gazette.
- Beleaguered businessman Strive Masiyiwa has applied to the High Court to bar the government from confiscating his Z$100 million cellular phone equipment or issuing any statements relating to it.
- The government has been advised to set up a regulatory authority which will set in motion the opening up of Zimbabwe's airwaves ahead of planned amendments to the Broadcasting Act.

- Zimbabwe stands to lose Z$8 billion repatriated over a 10-year period in management, franchise fees and dividends payments to the directors of Telecel which was recently awarded the country's second cellular phone licence.

- The government is due to engage an expatriate from Singapore to head the national airline, Air Zimbabwe, in a desperate move to steer the parastatal out of its financial and operational difficulties.

- Zimbabwe's first privately owned airline, Zimbabwe Express, has run into difficulties with delays in final authorisations while its chairman Elias Ngugama has resigned before the airline took to the skies.
- Premier Milling, a former milling giant which has been on the market for sale over the last two years, has still not found any takers.
- Nine people were killed and seven injured when a commuter omnibus crashed with a private car in southeastern Zimbabwe on Wednesday afternoon.
